core.text: When a verb does something to someone or something, the receiver of the action takes **the accusative (the object form)**, *cāsus accūsātīvus*: *Mārcus Iūliam pulsat* = Marcus hits Julia. The ending, not the position, tells you who is on the receiving end; *Iūliam Mārcus pulsat* means the same. The same form follows most prepositions (*ad*, *ante*, *post*, *per* …).
The object is what the verb acts on: *she hits him*. English shows it only in pronouns (*he / him*, *they / them*) and otherwise by putting the object after the verb. Latin marks every noun.
Singular adds -m (-am, -um, -em); plural adds -s (-ās, -ōs, -ēs). Neuter nouns keep their nominative shape: *oppidum* / *oppida* as object too.

*Puer puellam videt*: the word with -m is the one being seen. Swap the endings, *puerum puella videt*, and the girl is doing the seeing, whatever the English word order suggests. Neuter nouns are the one place the ending cannot help (*oppidum* is both); there the verb and common sense decide.

teach.title: What the object form does
teach.say: When a verb does something to someone, the one it is done to takes the accusative (the object form): *Iūlius Mārcum et Quīntum vocat* — Julius calls Marcus and Quintus. English shows this in a few pronouns (*he* / *him*) and otherwise by word order alone; Latin marks the noun itself, so the ending, not the place in the line, says who is on the receiving end.

teach.title: a-nouns: -am
teach.say: *Puella* (girl) becomes *puellam* when the verb acts on her: *Aemilia puellam parvam vocat*. One letter, -m, is the whole difference between doing and being done to.

teach.title: us-nouns: -um
teach.say: *Servus* (slave) becomes *servum*: *Iūlia servum improbum … videt*. The same -m does the work, added to -u instead of -a.

teach.title: More than one: -ōs, and -ās for a-nouns
teach.say: For several the mark is -s: us-nouns take -ōs (*servōs*) and a-nouns -ās (*puellās*). *Dominus servōs improbōs verberat* — the master beats the naughty slaves, every one of them carrying that -s. The us-noun’s cell is filled in for you; the a-noun’s is the one to write.

teach.title: Neuter nouns do not change at all
teach.say: *Oppidum* (town) is *oppidum* whether it acts or is acted on, and *oppida* is *oppida* either way: *Mārcus et Quīntus oppidum antīquum vident*. This is the one place where the ending cannot help you, and the verb and the sense have to decide.

teach.title: The ending, not the order
teach.say: *Puellam parvam māter laeta vocat* puts the object first and still means that the mother calls the girl, because *puellam* carries the -m. *Mārcus Quīntum pulsat, Quīntus Mārcum verberat* uses the same two names twice and swaps who does what by swapping the endings alone. Read the tails before you read the order.

more.text: From the learner's notes: a case is a form of a noun or pronoun that fixes its job in the sentence; English keeps cases only in pronouns (*I / me*, *who / whom*), Latin in nearly every noun. The nominative forms met so far (-a, -ae; -us, -ī; -um, -a; -is, -ēs) can only be subjects or rename a subject; masculine and feminine nouns make the accusative by adding -m in the singular and -s in the plural (*ūvam*, *ūvās*; *caseum*, *caseōs*; *pānem*, *pānēs*), neuters by changing nothing. The notes' examples with prepositions: *super petram* (on the rock), *contrā petram* (against the rock).

Ørberg cap. III gives -um / -am with the question *quem?* (whom?), and cap. V the plurals -ōs / -ās / -a. Pronouns: *mē*, *tē*, *eum*, *eam*, *eōs*, *eās*. The accusative also measures time and distance (*trēs hōrās* — for three hours) and, with towns and *domum*, says where to; some verbs take two accusatives (*mē rogat sententiam* — he asks me my opinion). A&G §387, §423.

sources: Ørberg cap. III & V Grammatica Latina
